lessons.title: The first law of thermodynamics and heat engines
lessons.programRef: GCE Advanced Level Physics — thermodynamics, cosmology, semiconductors (to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: State the first law Q = ΔU + W and calculate work done by a gas W = pΔV
Describe isothermal, isobaric, isochoric and adiabatic changes of an ideal gas
Explain the efficiency of a heat engine and the Carnot limit η = 1 − T_c/T_h
reviewNotes: Convention: W is the work done BY the gas (Q = ΔU + W); some boards use ΔU = Q + W (work done ON the gas) — check the board's convention.
Carnot efficiency, entropy and γ are probably beyond the core syllabus; flagged for the teacher.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: First law
blocks.md:
The **first law of thermodynamics** (conservation of energy): **Q = ΔU + W**, where Q is the heat supplied to the gas, ΔU the increase in its internal energy and W the work done **by** the gas. For a gas at constant pressure, **W = pΔV**; in general W is the area under the p–V graph.

For an ideal monatomic gas ΔU = (3/2)nRΔT (internal energy depends on T only).

blocks.title: Four special changes
blocks.md:
- **Isothermal** (T constant): ΔU = 0, so Q = W; W = nRT ln(V₂/V₁); pV = constant.
- **Isobaric** (p constant): W = pΔV; Q = (5/2)nRΔT for a monatomic gas.
- **Isochoric** (V constant): W = 0, so Q = ΔU = (3/2)nRΔT.
- **Adiabatic** (Q = 0): ΔU = −W; pV^γ = constant with γ = 5/3 for a monatomic gas; the gas cools when it expands.

blocks.caption: p–V graph: an isothermal curve (pV constant) and a steeper adiabatic curve from the same starting point.
blocks.alt: Two curves of pressure against volume starting at the same point, the adiabatic one falling more steeply than the isothermal one.

blocks.title: Heat engines
blocks.md: A **heat engine** takes heat Q_h from a hot reservoir, does work W and rejects heat Q_c to a cold reservoir: **η = W/Q_h = 1 − Q_c/Q_h**. No engine can convert all the heat to work (**second law**). The maximum (Carnot) efficiency for reservoirs at absolute temperatures T_h and T_c is **η = 1 − T_c/T_h**; real engines are less efficient.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Mixing the sign conventions: here W is work done **by** the gas (positive when the gas expands).
- Using °C in the Carnot efficiency: use kelvin.
- Thinking the temperature stays constant in an adiabatic change.
- Forgetting to convert dm³ or cm³ to m³ in W = pΔV.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Expansion at constant pressure
blocks.statement: A gas at 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa expands from 3.0 × 10⁻³ m³ to 5.0 × 10⁻³ m³ while absorbing 1200 J of heat. Find the work done and the change in internal energy.
steps: ΔU = Q − W = 1200 − 400 = 800 J (the internal energy increases, so the gas gets hotter).

blocks.title: Example 2 — Heating one mole
blocks.statement: One mole of monatomic gas is heated by 100 K, (a) at constant volume and (b) at constant pressure (R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹). Find Q in each case and the work in (b).
steps: (b) W = pΔV = RΔT = 831 J; ΔU is the same, 1246.5 J.
Q = ΔU + W = 1246.5 + 831 = 2077.5 J: more heat is needed at constant pressure.

lessons.title: Stars, redshift and the expanding Universe (to be checked against the syllabus)
lessons.programRef: GCE Advanced Level Physics — thermodynamics, cosmology, semiconductors (to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Use the inverse-square law for stellar flux and the Stefan–Boltzmann and Wien laws
Explain redshift, use z = Δλ/λ ≈ v/c and state Hubble's law v = H₀d
Describe the evidence for the Big Bang and the expanding Universe
reviewNotes: THIS LESSON MAY NOT BE ON THE CAMEROON GCE ADVANCED LEVEL SYLLABUS: it is included as optional enrichment and must be checked by a teacher.
H₀ ≈ 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹ and L_Sun = 3.8 × 10²⁶ W are rounded values. The Hubble plot points are illustrative, not real data.
Black holes and dark matter are not covered.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Stars as black bodies
blocks.md: A star of luminosity (power output) L at distance d gives a flux (intensity) **F = L/4πd²** (inverse-square law). A hot body radiates a spectrum with a peak wavelength given by **Wien's law: λ_max T = 2.90 × 10⁻³ m K**; the total power radiated by a star of radius R and surface temperature T is **L = 4πR²σT⁴** (Stefan–Boltzmann; σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴).

blocks.title: Redshift and Hubble's law
blocks.md:
Light from receding sources is shifted to longer wavelengths (**Doppler redshift**): z = Δλ/λ ≈ v/c for v ≪ c. Distant galaxies show redshifts proportional to their distance: **Hubble's law v = H₀d** with H₀ ≈ 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹ (1 Mpc ≈ 3.09 × 10¹⁹ km). This means that space itself is expanding.

The quantity 1/H₀ gives an estimate of the age of the Universe (about 1.4 × 10¹⁰ years).
blocks.tex: F=\frac{L}{4\pi d^{2}}\quad L=4\pi R^{2}\sigma T^{4}\quad v=H_0d

blocks.caption: Hubble's law: recession velocity against distance for galaxies (illustrative points, line v = 70d).
blocks.alt: A scatter of points close to a straight line through the origin showing velocity increasing with distance.

blocks.title: Evidence for the Big Bang
blocks.md: The Universe began in a hot, dense state about 14 billion years ago and has been expanding and cooling. Evidence: (1) the **redshift of galaxies**; (2) the **cosmic microwave background** radiation, a nearly uniform glow at about 2.7 K; (3) the observed proportions of hydrogen and helium. Values such as H₀ are still being refined and different methods give slightly different values.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Forgetting to convert km and Mpc to a common unit when finding the age (1/H₀).
- Using °C for the temperature in Wien's or Stefan–Boltzmann law: use kelvin.
- Thinking galaxies move away from a centre: every observer sees others receding.
- Assuming the redshift is caused by the light being 'tired': it is due to the expansion of space.

blocks.title: Example 1 — The Sun
blocks.statement: The Sun's luminosity is 3.8 × 10²⁶ W. (a) Find the flux at the Earth (1.5 × 10¹¹ m). (b) The peak wavelength of sunlight is about 500 nm: find the surface temperature, then the radius of the Sun.

blocks.title: Example 2 — A distant galaxy
blocks.statement: A galaxy's light has Δλ/λ = 0.010. Find its recession speed and its distance (c = 3.00 × 10⁵ km/s, H₀ = 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹).

objectives: Describe intrinsic and extrinsic (n-type, p-type) semiconductors and the action of a p–n junction diode, including the LED

Describe a transistor or logic gate as a switch (qualitative)
reviewNotes: Transistor and logic-gate content is only qualitative and may be examined differently; band theory is simplified.
Op-amp lessons may be outside the board's syllabus at this level: check.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Semiconductors and the diode
blocks.md:
In a **semiconductor** (silicon, germanium) the resistance falls as the temperature rises, because more charge carriers are released. **Doping** adds impurities: **n-type** (extra electrons, e.g. phosphorus) and **p-type** (extra 'holes', e.g. boron).

A **p–n junction** has a **depletion layer**. Forward-biased (p to +), it conducts above about 0.6 V (silicon); reverse-biased it conducts almost nothing. Applications: rectifiers; **light-emitting diodes** emit photons of energy about equal to the band gap (E = hc/λ).

blocks.title: The ideal operational amplifier
blocks.md:
An **op-amp** has two inputs (− inverting, + non-inverting) and one output. Ideal properties: infinite open-loop gain, infinite input resistance, zero output resistance. With negative feedback the two inputs are at the **same potential**, and no current enters the inputs.

**Inverting amplifier**: V_out = −(R_f/R_in)V_in. **Non-inverting amplifier**: V_out = (1 + R_f/R₁)V_in. The output cannot exceed the supply rails: it **saturates**.

blocks.caption: An inverting op-amp amplifier: V_out = −(R_f/R_in)V_in.
blocks.alt: A triangular amplifier symbol with an input resistor to the inverting input, a feedback resistor from the output back to that input, and the non-inverting input earthed.

blocks.title: Switching circuits
blocks.md: A **transistor** (npn) acts as a switch: when the base–emitter voltage exceeds about 0.6 V the collector–emitter path conducts and a relay, lamp or buzzer in the collector circuit can be switched on. A potential divider with an LDR or thermistor can supply the base voltage (light- or temperature-operated switch). **Logic gates** (AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR) process digital signals (0 or 1); NOT gives the opposite of its input.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Forgetting the series resistor for an LED: without it the current is too high.
- Using the inverting formula without the minus sign.
- Ignoring saturation: the output can never be larger than the supply voltage.
- Thinking current flows into an ideal op-amp input.

blocks.title: Example 1 — An LED
blocks.statement: A red LED emits light of wavelength 650 nm. Estimate the energy gap. The LED needs 2.0 V and 20 mA from a 5.0 V supply: find the series resistor.
steps: The resistor takes 5.0 − 2.0 = 3.0 V at 0.020 A: R = 3.0/0.020 = 150 Ω.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Amplifiers
blocks.statement: An inverting amplifier has R_in = 10 kΩ and R_f = 100 kΩ. Find V_out for V_in = +0.30 V. What would a non-inverting amplifier with R₁ = 10 kΩ and R_f = 90 kΩ give for the same input?

objectives: Plan an investigation: identify independent, dependent and control variables, choose apparatus and reduce uncertainty
Linearise relationships (y = mx + c) and find physical quantities from gradients and intercepts, with uncertainties
Evaluate an experiment: sources of error and improvements
reviewNotes: The graphs shown use generated data with t½ = 20 min exactly; real data would scatter.
The board's practical assessment (continuous assessment, practical examination) format is not described; check.
Instrument precision values are typical (micrometer 0.01 mm, vernier 0.1 mm).
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Planning
blocks.md: In a good investigation you state the **independent variable** (changed), the **dependent variable** (measured) and the **control variables** (kept constant). Plan to take a **range** of at least five values, repeat readings, choose instruments of suitable precision (micrometer 0.01 mm for wire diameter, vernier caliper 0.1 mm or better, stopwatch for **many** oscillations to reduce reaction-time error), and include a safety consideration.

blocks.title: Linearising a relationship
blocks.md:
Rearrange the equation into **y = mx + c** so that a straight-line graph gives the unknown from the gradient m or intercept c:

- T = 2π√(l/g) → plot **T² against l**: gradient = 4π²/g.
- N = N₀e^(−λt) → plot **ln N against t**: gradient = −λ.
- y = kxⁿ → plot **lg y against lg x**: gradient = n, intercept = lg k.
- V = E − Ir → plot V against I: intercept E, gradient −r.

blocks.caption: Linearised decay data: ln A against t gives a straight line of gradient −λ.
blocks.alt: Five points on a downward sloping straight line of the natural logarithm of count rate against time.

blocks.title: Graphs and uncertainty
blocks.md: Choose scales that fill more than half the graph, label axes with quantities **and units**, plot points accurately, draw a best-fit line with points balanced above and below. Find the gradient using a **large triangle** on the line (not data points). The uncertainty in the gradient comes from the steepest and shallowest acceptable lines: Δm = ½(m_max − m_min). Use percentage uncertainties to decide which measurement limits accuracy.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Calculating the gradient from two data points that are close together.
- Forgetting units on axis labels or in the gradient.
- Calling an unavoidable random scatter a 'human error': name the specific source (for example, reaction time when starting the stopwatch).
- Changing more than one variable at a time.

blocks.title: Example 1 — g from a pendulum
blocks.statement: A student measures the period T for lengths l = 0.20 to 1.00 m and plots T² against l. T² = 0.81 s² at 0.20 m and 4.04 s² at 1.00 m (two points on the best-fit line). Find g.
steps: T² = (4π²/g) l, so g = 4π²/gradient = 39.48/4.04 = 9.77 m s⁻².

blocks.title: Example 2 — Half-life by a straight line
blocks.statement: Corrected count rates fall from 800 to 200 counts/min in 40 min. A graph of ln A against t has a gradient of −0.0347 min⁻¹ . Find the half-life.
steps: ln A = ln A₀ − λt, so the gradient is −λ and λ = 0.0347 min⁻¹.
t½ = ln 2/λ = 0.693/0.0347 = 20.0 min (check: 800 → 400 → 200 in two half-lives of 20 min).
